name: Christoffer Bodegård
bio:
Christoffer Bodegård is a game developer, writer, and fan of interactive storytelling.
Creator of Esoteric Ebb.

If the pair would overlap, both shrink by the same factor, but never below the minimum.

work.title: The Next Project?
paragraphs: We'll see what I'll be working on in the future. Very exciting.

work.title: Esoteric Ebb
paragraphs: ESOTERIC EBB is an isometric CRPG I've been working on as a side project since 2018. Inspired by games like Planescape Torment and Disco Elysium, EBB is all about social exploration, magical encounters, and personal revelations. It started as an excuse for me to do what I enjoy most in game development: writing interactive and dynamic dialogs.

work.title: Gori: Cuddly Carnage
paragraphs: I collaborated with Angry Demon Studio on Gori during the start of the project, and was a fierce supporter for the rest of development. It launched in 2024, and I'm very impressed with the direction they took. Funny, irreverent, and with a very distinct style in both gameplay and writing, I'm very happy to have been a small part of it.

work.title: Raft
paragraphs: Between 2021-2022 I was hired by Redbeet Interactive to take on the task of restructuring, writing, and concluding the narrative of their game Raft.

This included creating over 600 lines of voice recorded dialog. Around half of these were for collectable story 'notes', and the other half for NPC encountered towards the end of the game. The people at Redbeet were wonderful to work with, and it was amazing to get a glimpse into their development process during my time with them.

work.title: Apsulov: End of Gods
paragraphs: I worked on Apsulov: End of Gods from June 2018 until release in August 2019. The tagline 'future viking horror' was used to pitch the project to me, and it immediately set the tone for my writing. The game is all about bleak science fiction with apocalyptic consequences, mixed with dark themes of Norse myth.
Apsulov: End of Gods was co-written with John Kalderon, and developed by the amazing people at Angry Demon Studio.

paragraphs: I was invited to host a workshop at Nordic. A so-called MASTERCLASS, in which I went over a more freestyled version of my interactive writing talk, along with almost three hours of QnA! A ton of great questions and always fun to rant - especially since this was right after the release of Ebb!

talks.linkLabel: PLEASE (DON'T) MAKE MORE GAMES WITH INTERACTIVE WRITING
paragraphs: I've been desperately trying to understand interactive storytelling for years. As I dove into the topic, I stumbled upon a problem: there was no common term for the thing I wanted to do. The thing that Planescape: Torment and Disco Elysium did so well. So I called it 'INTERACTIVE WRITING', which technically already means something entirely different, and this talk goes over my initial exploration of why I needed this term, along with a list of general rules of agency I follow in my personal design philosophy.
None of my talks have been recorded yet, which is probably for the best. But since it was pretty well-received at the conference, some people asked me to make the slides public. Here's the link:

chapters.title: University of Skövde
paragraphs: I've always been lazy. The one time in my life I decided to actually put in some effort was when I landed on the last spot of the Game Writing class of 2015. I was told (as I should have been) that 'Game Writers' have a very difficult time landing jobs- so I made sure I learned programming and graphical design over those years, teaching myself the basics of game development.

As I did, I ended up falling deep into the rabbit hole of interactive storytelling. I wrote both my bachelor's and my master's on the topic of agency and UI design in CRPGs, attempting to answer one simple question: How do you write good choices?

chapters.title: Freelancing
paragraphs: As I finished my studies, I did not get a job. As a result, I did what many a gamedev student do: I became an entrepreneur. Grabbing some of my fellow aspiring devs, we joined the local incubator program at Science Park Skövde. For about a year we tried making a few different games- but it didn't work out. I learned a hell of a lot from the experience though. I also ended up with some contacts, which led me to becoming a freelance writer and developer.

Over these years, I had the opportunity to work on a handful of titles (some of which even released) and managed to create a somewhat stable existence. However, for all the cool writing gigs I got, my obsession with interactive storytelling led me to spend all my spare time on my own project, called EBBRPG. Started in 2018 as my naive attempt at a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, it slowly took over my life. By 2022, when my gigs dried up, I started going full-time at my new company.

chapters.title: Sudden Snail
paragraphs: I technically never chose to go full-time on Ebb. I actively looked for other jobs until mid-2023, simply because I did not see a production like this going anywhere. Solo developer, refusing any help. Massive scale CRPG. Half a million words of dialogs. It sounds delusional. But at the start of 2022, I managed to clear the biggest hurdle: I found an art style. Then I nailed a story I really, really believed in. After that, every time I showed the game to someone, the response was increasingly positive.

At the end of 2022, I once again entered the incubator program, rejoining the wonderful local Sweden Game Arena community. I'd been working from home for years at this point, cooped up in my dark shack, alone. Taking that step outside woke me up to the possibilities I had: I could actually turn Ebb into a job.

I pitched to publishers all throughout 2023, as the game (and I) got progressively better. At the start of 2024, my first demo blew up thanks to a PC Gamer article, and within a month I'd gotten five contracts to choose from. I picked Raw Fury. Since then, thanks to having an actual budget, I've been collaborating with a ton of amazing artists. If things go my way, I'm looking to make a long career by making games with a ton of interactive writing, interesting political themes, and characters that matter. Maybe some jokes too, if I'm feeling frisky.

items.title: Heroes of Might and Magic 3
why: This one is special, as a lot of people would agree. I play strategy and RPGs, that's my thing. I like to branch out into all genres to some degree, but these two I'm obsessed with - and Heroes 3 is the reason why. It's a game I've played so much during my childhood that it's ingrained into my psyche - to me it's the fantasy aesthetic perfected. There is no better creature design. There is no better music. I'm playing through the campaign again, whenever I have time to spare, and it's always a complete joy to the senses.

items.title: Planescape: Torment
why: I've written essays at Uni about why this game succeeds. It's a spectacle. The type of experience that rightfully stands as iconic within interactive writing, and it's the game that ruined RPGs for me. After playing PS:T in High School, my standards rose to the point where I felt like nothing I played - or created - was ever good enough. And that spark, that's what made me keep going for all these years. To iterate until I'd made something that seemed at least decent in comparison. This game was a formative experience for me. It lives in my heart, and it is my benchmark.

items.title: Disco Elysium
why: Motherfucker. They did it. 2018->2019 was a weird pair of years for me. I went from burnt-out, to madly inspired, to completely devoid of creativity, all because I got this idea of making a 'D&D simulation' based on the best parts of PS:T. But I couldn't do it, not as a solo developer, at least not without failing hard at combat. And obviously, you can't make a CRPG without combat. Then, Disco Elysium. Within thirty minutes of playing it, I knew that these absolute geniuses managed to solve every single problem I had in my design document, while also doing it without traditional combat. I finished the game in three days, skipping work to do it. Then I spent the following months analyzing, researching, and trying to understand exactly how and why they managed to revolutionize RPG design. It changed my life. Almost ruined it as well, which is pretty Disco.

items.title: Super Mario Galaxy
why: BING BING! WAHOO! I'm actually a big Nintendo guy. I was one of those losers who had a Wii instead of a 360, and man did I stick with it. And after all this time, it is still Galaxy that stands as my number one platformer, for design reasons, but also - in all honesty - because of the gloriously aesthetic experience. The music, the VIBES, the visuals, the pacing of it - everything just OOZES perfection. I really love most big Mario games, and I've played them all. But this one? This is mine.

items.title: Deus Ex
why: Holy shit, talk about games that leave an impression. I first found out about Deus Ex from a copy of Swedish PC Gamer, wherein they wrote a fun exploration (or guide) on the first level, the Statue of Liberty. It's crazy how just talking about the many hundreds of different solutions that exist in this 'tutorial level' manages to sell it so well. Looking at it as a kid, it just seemed like another old FPS game, one that was hard to parse and approach. But once you get past that initial step, once you GET the freedom and extreme level of interaction/reactivity that lives here, then you just can't look away. I long to one day live up to this level of systemic storytelling, branching narrative, and complete player agency.

items.title: The Secret of Monkey Island
why: Something about narrative lets games live far beyond their years. When it's done right. This is a game where they did everything right, in a time when it was NOT something to take for granted. It spawned a legacy that still burns today, and it's obvious why the second you boot it up. I tend to split up games into two abstract categories - aesthetic games and mechanical games. As in, which games sell because they offer a vibe and which games sell because they offer number-go-up. This is the fundamental basis of that first one, and I recommend anyone trying to sell a game based on aesthetics to play this at least once in their life.

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
why: I first played it during the Gamecube era, the Master Quest edition or whatever. Just one out of many old games I played during that time of my childhood, as the newer games were a bit too expensive and I had a huge library to get through. But OoT is really special. I'm a bit too young to be a Link to the Past person, and Majora's Mask didn't really get to me until I was a bit older. But OoT is to me an experience that exemplified the early 3D era. What they could do with the mechanics, the narrative, the fantasy of it. How it spawned an entire genre of clones within its own game series, only breaking upon Breath of the Wild over twenty years later. This is an iconic game that just lives rent-free in my head.

items.title: 999: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors
why: I've played a lot of Visual Novels. I've played a lot of DS games. I did not expect this to be as influential as it was when I started it. I do like Death Games as a genre. There's just something special about putting a bunch of characters in an almost abstractly stressful situation and seeing how they manage - and I would say this game was the hinge that brought timelines-as-game-mechanics into the mainstream. Which, while a bit played out today, still clearly lingers as a mark on the industry.

items.title: Crusader Kings 3
why: I love Paradox games. I mean, it's a bit of a complicated relationship, but in the last fifteen years I have given a large portion of my spare time to painting these damn maps. EU4 is the one I've got the most time in, while VIC3 is my current favorite. But, Crusader Kings 3 is the one that I consider to be the best: solid design. It's accessible. It's essentially a dollhouse of numbers that come alive. It manages to have the best UI and visuals of all grand-strats to this day. It's also terrible. I've got more hours in CK2. But here's the thing: nothing about this game makes me think that it's going backwards. And everything they've done so far makes it obvious to me that once they release just a few more expansions, then it'll far, far surpass the heights of its predecessor. I'm writing this in mid-2026 though, so maybe it'll turn to shit in the end. But that's the beauty and horror of Paradox's whole DLC setup. It's like a mystery box. Why wouldn't you want to check inside? The next update could be the best one yet!

items.title: World of Warcraft
why: I like WoW for very different reasons than a lot of people. I don't like the progression systems. I don't like the endless content cycles. I don't like any of the narratives post-TBC. Nevertheless, that original world they created... I guess you should call it 'Classic WoW' - it was perfect. It was as close as a fictional world has ever gotten to reaching the peak of aesthetic perfection. The visuals, expanded from the already wonderful WC3 designs. The music and audio design. The tastefully stylized, yet grounded animation style. And of course, that wonderful mix of 90s era FRICTION-design, with the faster-paced (and far more addicting) SMOOTH-design of our modern day industry. I don't believe Classic WoW was a period in time that you cannot return to. I simply believe the balance they struck here (some accidentally, some by masterful execution) was pure genius. I'm very happy that no one has ever managed to recreate that wonder in a world that doesn't destroy itself with a focus on number-go-up gameplay. Otherwise, I never would have had the time to make a career for myself. Azeroth, while not perfect, is the standard I hold in my mind for what an online living world should be at its minimum.

items.title: Baldur's Gate 2: Shadows of Amn
why: BG1 is purer in a sense, but it only ends up in my top 30, maybe. BG2 is just far too impressive to ignore. The expansive narrative, the way it builds upon BG1 in such a bold way, the fact that it is still to this day one of the LARGEST RPGs ever made... It's a masterpiece, and still holds up to this day. It is also the only D&D game that has ever even gotten close to simulating late-stage, high-level D&D play. Maybe one day I'll be able to do the same.

esoteric.title: Esoteric Inspirations
esoteric.intro: One of those classic questions is always: what inspired you? I tend to always give different answers depending on my mood, so don't consider this a finished list or anything - BUT, here's a little compilation of the various pieces of media that I would consider as living in the back of my skull during the development of everything ESOTERIC.

notes: As for visuals and audio, I'm far more inclined to let those live within the skulls of my collaborators. My job mainly revolves around writing/programming/design, as well as compiling and integrating all the 'assets' my wonderful artists create. Therefore, if you want to find out more what makes, for example, Oscar Westberg's artwork look the way it does, or how Anders Bach approaches his idea of this esoteric music - feel free to look them up and ask them yourself. Or just drop a question in the Discord, they tend to hang out there sometimes.
Oh, and of course: Lord of the Rings and D&D, along with a thousand iterations of TTRPGs and fantasy stories that coagulate into inspiring the rest of what has become this ESOTERIC ERA.
